documentNotes.title: Full native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface This publication contains 39 theoretical and 14 practical competition problems from the 41st – 45th International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 2009 – 2013. It has been published by the IChO International Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) as a continuation of the preceding Volumes 1 and 2 published on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the IChO with the titles: • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 1, 1st – 20th IChO, 1968 – 1988 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2008). • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 2, 21st – 40th IChO, 1989 – 2008 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2009). Not less than 318 theoretical and 110 practical problems were set in the IChO during the forty-five years of its existence. In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems (numbering the tasks of the particular problems, solution inserted immediately after the text of the problem, solutions without grading points and special graphs used for grading of practical problems). Nevertheless, the mentioned corrections and changes do not concern the contents and language of the competition problems. The practical problems set in the IChO competitions, contain as a rule some instructions, list of apparatuses available, chemicals on each desk and those available in the laboratory, and the risk and safety phrases with regard to the chemicals used. All of these items are important for the competitors during the competition but less important for those who are going to read the competition tasks of this collection and thus, they are omitted. Some parts of the solutions of practical problems are also left out since they require the experimental data which could be obtained by experiments during the practical part of the IChO competition. In this publication SI quantities and units are preferred. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI. Although the numbers of significant figures in the results of some solutions do not obey the criteria generally accepted, they were left without change.

Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and due to the procedure of creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to assign any author's name to a particular problem. Nevertheless, responsibility for the scientific content and language of the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry Olympiads. This review of the competition problems from the 41st – 45th IChO should serve to both competitors and their teachers as a source of further ideas in their preparation for this difficult competition. For those who have taken part in some of these International Chemistry Olympiads the collection of the problems could be of help as archival and documentary material. In the previous forty-five years many known and unknown people - teachers, authors, pupils, and organizers proved their abilities and knowledge and contributed to the success of this already well known and world-wide competition. We wish to all who will organize and attend the future International Chemistry Olympiads, success and happiness. Bratislava, July 2014 Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Theoretical problem 1 — Clathrate gun
problems.statement:
*The only gun that is able to kill all living people in one shot*

On the floors of oceans and seas there are vast reserves of methane in the form of clathrate compounds called methane hydrates. These reserves can be mined and serve as a source of energy or raw materials for organic synthesis. However, scientists are seriously worried about the possibility of spontaneous decomposition of hydrates caused by the raising ocean temperature. It is believed that if a sufficient amount of methane is released into the atmosphere, the oceans will warm up quicker due to the greenhouse effect, further accelerating the decomposition of clathrates. Due to the explosion of the resulting methane-air mixture and/or changes in the composition of the atmosphere, all living creatures may become extinct. This apocalyptic scenario is called a clathrate gun.

[figure: p1-fig1]

Upon decomposition of 1.00 g of a methane hydrate with a fixed composition at 25 °C and atmospheric (101.3 kPa) pressure, 205 cm³ of methane is released.

parts.statement: Determine n (not necessarily integer) in the formula of methane hydrate, CH₄·nH₂O.
parts.statementAfter: Real methane hydrate has a non-stoichiometric composition close to CH₄·6H₂O. At atmospheric pressure, methane hydrate decomposes at −81 °C. However, under high pressures (e.g. on the ocean floor) it is stable at much higher temperatures. Decomposition of methane hydrate produces gaseous methane and solid or liquid water depending on temperature.

parts.statement: Write down the equation of decomposition of 1 mol of CH₄·6H₂O producing solid water (ice) H₂O(s).
parts.statementAfter: The enthalpy of this process equals 17.47 kJ mol⁻¹. Assume that the enthalpies do not depend on temperature and pressure, the volume change upon decomposition of hydrate is equal to the volume of released methane, and methane is an ideal gas.

parts.statement: At what external pressure does decomposition of methane hydrate into methane and ice take place at −5 °C?

What is the minimum possible depth of pure liquid water at which methane hydrates can be stable? To answer this question, you should first deduce at which minimum temperature methane hydrate can coexist with liquid water. Choose the correct answer.

□ 272.9 K; □ 273.15 K; □ 273.4 K.
parts.statementAfter: Large methane hydrate stocks on the floor of Baikal lake, the largest freshwater lake in Russia and in the world, have been discovered in July 2009 by the crew of a deep-submergence vehicle «Mir-2». During the ascent from the depth of 1400 m methane hydrate samples started to decompose at the depth of 372 m.

parts.statement: Determine the temperature in Baikal lake at the depth of 372 m. The enthalpy of fusion of ice is equal to 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.statementAfter: Total amount of methane in hydrates on the Earth is no less than 5×10¹¹ tons.

parts.statement: By how many degrees would the Earth atmosphere heat up, if such amount of methane is burned by reacting with atmospheric oxygen? The enthalpy of combustion of methane is −889 kJ mol⁻¹, the total heat capacity of the Earth’s atmosphere is about 4×10²¹ J K⁻¹.

solution.statement:
**1.1** By the ideal gas law, the amount of methane ν = pV/(RT) = (101300×205×10⁻⁶)/(8.314×298.15) = 8.38×10⁻³ mol. The amount of water in hydrate ν = (1 − 8.38×10⁻³×16)/18 = 4.81×10⁻² mol. The ratio of amounts of water and methane is (4.81×10⁻²)/(8.38×10⁻³) ≈ 5.75, i.e. the composition is CH₄·5.75H₂O or xCH₄·5.75xH₂O, where x is any natural number.

**1.2** CH₄·6H₂O = CH₄ + 6H₂O.

**1.3** Decomposition can be viewed as a phase transition obeying the Clausius–Clapeyron equation: dp/dT = ΔH/(TΔV).

ΔV = RT/p + 6M(H₂O(s))/ρ(H₂O(s)) − M(CH₄·6H₂O)/ρ(CH₄·6H₂O).

The difference between the last two terms is negligibly small compared with the first. Thus (1/p)dp = (ΔH/(RT²))dT, giving p = p₀ exp[(ΔH/R)(1/T₀ − 1/T)]. Substituting T₀ = 192.15 K, T = 268.15 K, p₀ = 1 atm gives p = 22 atm or 2.2 MPa. Correct answer: p = 2.2 MPa.

**1.4** Correct answer: ☑ 272.9 K. At the minimum possible depth, atmosphere plus water-column pressure equals the dissociation pressure of methane hydrate. The temperature must be as low as possible but cannot be less than the melting point of water at that pressure. Thus temperature and pressure correspond to coexistence of water, ice, methane hydrate and gaseous methane. Since the melting point of water decreases with increasing pressure, the correct answer is 272.9 K. Substituting T = 272.9 K gives p = 2.58 MPa. Water-column height h = (p − p_atm)/(gρ(H₂O)), g = 9.8 m s⁻²; hence h ≈ 250 m.

**1.5** By Hess’s law, the process CH₄·6H₂O = CH₄ + 6H₂O(l) has enthalpy 17.47 + 6×6.01 = 53.53 kJ mol⁻¹. An equilibrium between methane, water and methane hydrate is established at T₀ = 272.9 K and p₀ = 2.58 MPa. Calculate decomposition temperature T at pressure p = 9.8×1000×372 + 101000 = 3746600 Pa using 1/T = 1/T₀ + (R/ΔH)ln(p₀/p). The obtained temperature is T = 277.3 K or about 4 °C (in agreement with measured Baikal water temperature at this depth).

**1.6** Burning methane releases [(500×10⁹×10³)/0.016]×889×10³ = 2.78×10²² J. The atmosphere heats up by (2.78×10²²)/(4×10²¹) ≈ 7 K. ΔT = 7 K.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 2 — Break down photosynthesis – the Hill reaction
problems.statement: In the history of photosynthesis research, there were some breakthrough experiments which added much to our knowledge of this very complex process. One of such experiments was performed in 1930s by an English biochemist Robert Hill. In this problem, we consider some of his data together with the data of more recent experiments.

parts.statement: In plants, under illumination, carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrates (denote as $\{\mathrm{CH_2O}\}$) and oxygen is produced. Write the overall equation of photosynthesis in plants.
parts.statementAfter: Much of the photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts – organelles found in plant cells and containing chlorophyll – the light-absorbing substance. Hill isolated chloroplasts from the cells by grinding the leaves in the sucrose solutions. The cell-free chloroplasts did not produce oxygen under illumination even in the presence of CO₂. However, upon adding potassium ferrioxalate K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃] (with the excess of potassium oxalate) to the chloroplast suspension Hill observed oxygen liberation under illumination even without CO₂.

parts.statement: Hill’s experiment enabled to determine the source of oxygen during photosynthesis. Write the formulas of the oxidant and the reducing agent in the photosynthesis inside the plant cells and in the cell-free chloroplasts (the Hill reaction).
parts.statementAfter:
Hill measured the amount of evolved oxygen using muscle haemoglobin (Hill denoted it Hb) which binds all molecular oxygen in a 1:1 ratio to form HbO₂. The initial concentration of Hb was 0.6×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³. Kinetic curves corresponding to different ferrioxalate concentrations are shown in the figure (the upper curve corresponds to 2.0×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³).

[figure: p2-fig1]

The fraction of bound haemoglobin HbO₂ (with respect to the initial amount of Hb) as a function of time. Crosses denote the end of the reaction. Figure 2a from R. Hill, Oxygen produced by isolated chloroplasts, Proc. R. Soc. B, 1939, v.127, pp.192–210.

parts.label: 2.3a
parts.statement: From the figure, estimate the Fe/O₂ mole ratio at the end of the reaction. Do not take into account the iron from Hb.

parts.label: 2.3b
parts.statement: Write the equation of Hill reaction assuming that it proceeds with a high yield.

parts.label: 2.3c
parts.statement:
Using the table of standard electrode potentials, determine the Gibbs energy of the Hill reaction at T = 298 K, oxygen pressure 1 mm Hg, pH = 8 and standard concentrations of other species. Is this reaction spontaneous at such conditions?

| Half-reaction | E° / V |
|---|---|
| O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e → 2H₂O | +1.23 |
| CO₂ + 4H⁺ + 8e → $\{\mathrm{CH_2O}\}$ + H₂O | −0.01 |
| Fe³⁺ + e → Fe²⁺ | +0.77 |
| Fe³⁺ + 3e → Fe⁰ | −0.04 |
| [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ + e → [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]⁴⁻ | +0.05 |
| [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]⁴⁻ + 2e → Fe + 3C₂O₄²⁻ | −0.59 |

Source note: the CO₂ half-reaction prints 8e; that native coefficient is retained.
parts.statementAfter:
Now, the name “Hill reaction” denotes photochemical oxidation of water by any oxidant other than carbon dioxide which is sensitized by plant cells or isolated chloroplasts.

In another experiment (1952), quinone in an acid solution was used as an oxidant in the Hill reaction initiated by light flashes in the Chlorella algae. Experimental data are shown in the figure. The volume of oxygen (in mm³, at temperature 10 °C and pressure 740 mm Hg) per one gram of chlorophyll per one flash was determined as a function of light intensity for natural photosynthesis and for isolated chloroplasts. It was found that the maximum yield of oxygen is the same for natural photosynthesis and the Hill reaction.

[figure: p2-fig2]

Figure 1 from H. Ehrmantraut, E. Rabinovitch, Kinetics of Hill reaction, Archives of Biochemistry and Biophysics, 1952, v.38, pp.67–84.

parts.label: 2.4a
parts.statement: Determine the reaction order of a photochemical Hill reaction with respect to light intensity at low and high intensity. For each case choose one of the following three values: 0, 1 or 2.

parts.label: 2.4b
parts.statement: How many chlorophyll molecules participate in the formation of one oxygen molecule in the saturation limit of the Hill reaction? The molecular mass of chlorophyll is about 900 Da.
parts.statementAfter: The quantum requirement of the light redox reactions is defined as the average number of light photons (not necessarily integer) needed for the transfer of one electron from a reducing agent to an oxidant. The isolated chloroplasts were irradiated during 2 hours by a monochromatic light (wavelength 672 nm) with the energy input 0.503 mJ s⁻¹, and the total volume of oxygen formed was 47.6 mm³ (under the same conditions as in question 4).

parts.statement: Calculate the quantum requirement for the Hill reaction.

Try to make conclusions from the above experiments (questions 2.2–2.5). Tick the relevant boxes.

[figure: p2-fig3]

solution.statement:
**2.1** H₂O + CO₂ = $\{\mathrm{CH_2O}\}$ + O₂.

**2.2**

| Process | Oxidant | Reducing agent |
|---|---|---|
| Natural photosynthesis | CO₂ | H₂O |
| Hill reaction | K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃] | H₂O |

**2.3a** The upper curve in the saturation limit gives ~75% of HbO₂. n(Fe)/n(O₂) = c(Fe)/c(HbO₂) = (2.0×10⁻⁴)/(0.75×0.6×10⁻⁴) = 4.4/1.

**2.3b** Ratio ~4:1 shows Fe(III) reduced to Fe(II), existing as a complex in excess oxalate: 2H₂O + 4[Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ → O₂ + 4[Fe(C₂O₄)₃]⁴⁻ + 4H⁺.

**2.3c** [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ + e → [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]⁴⁻, E₁° = 0.05 V; O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e → 2H₂O, E₂° = 1.23 V. E° = E₁° − E₂° = −1.18 V.

ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln(pO₂[H⁺]⁴) = −4×96500×(−1.18) + 8.314×298×ln[(1/750)(1×10⁻⁸)⁴] = 2.57×10⁵ J mol⁻¹ = 257 kJ mol⁻¹. The reaction is highly endoergic and hence not spontaneous. Light is necessary.

Source note: the key's numerical expression uses the printed oxygen fraction 1/750, while the question specifies 1 mm Hg; this literal key expression is retained.

**2.4a** Reaction order at low intensity: 1; at high intensity: 0.

**2.4b** n(Chl)/n(O₂) = (1/900)/[(12×10⁻⁶×(740/760)×101.3)/(8.314×283)] = 2200.

**2.5** Total energy absorbed E = 0.503×10⁻³×3600×2 = 3.62 J. Energy of one mole of photons E_m = hcN_A/λ = (6.63×10⁻³⁴×3.00×10⁸×6.02×10²³)/(672×10⁻⁹) = 1.78×10⁵ J mol⁻¹. n(phot) = E/E_m = 2.03×10⁻⁵ mol.

n(O₂) = pV/(RT) = [(740/760)×101.3×47.6×10⁻⁶]/(8.314×283) = 2.00×10⁻⁶ mol. Formation of one mole of O₂ requires transfer of 4 electrons: n(e) = 8.00×10⁻⁶ mol. Quantum requirement n(phot)/n(e) = 2.5.

**2.6**

| Statement | Yes | No |
|---|---|---|
| In natural photosynthesis, water oxidation and CO₂ reduction are separated in space. | ✓ | |
| In chloroplasts, O₂ is produced from CO₂. | | ✓ |
| Oxidation of water in chloroplasts requires light illumination. | ✓ | |
| Most of chlorophylls in chloroplasts participate directly in the photochemical O₂ production. | | ✓ |
| In isolated chloroplasts, every absorbed photon causes transfer of one electron. | | ✓ |

problems.title: Theoretical problem 3 — Meerwein-Schmidt-Ponndorf-Verley reaction
problems.statement:
Meerwein-Schmidt-Ponndorf-Verley (MSPV) reaction is a useful tool for reduction of carbonyl compounds to alcohols. The reaction is the reduction of carbonyl compounds by low molecular weight alcohols in the presence of alkoxides of aluminium or other metals:

[figure: p3-fig1]

The mechanism of the reaction includes coordination of carbonyl compound by aluminium alkoxide, hydride transfer in the inner sphere of the complex and subsequent transalkoxylation. It can be schematically represented as follows (transalkoxylation is shown as a one-step process for brevity):

[figure: p3-fig2]

The reaction is reversible and shifting the equilibrium to the desired product requires some excess of the reductant. In some cases (e.g. in the case of reduction of aromatic aldehydes and ketones) the equilibrium constant is so large that the reverse reaction can be neglected.

The table below contains standard entropies and standard enthalpies of formation of liquid substances at 298 K. The boiling points of the substances at 1 bar are also given.

| Substance | ΔfH°₂₉₈ / kJ mol⁻¹ | S°₂₉₈ / J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | t_vap / °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acetone | −248.4 | 200.4 | 56 |
| Isopropanol | −318.1 | 180.6 | 82 |
| Cyclohexanone | −271.2 | 229.0 | 156 |
| Cyclohexanol | −348.2 | 203.4 | 161 |

parts.label: 3.1a
parts.statement: Calculate the minimum isopropanol to cyclohexanone mass ratio which is required to reach a 99% yield of reaction at 298 K. Assume that: i) the reaction mixture eventually gets at equilibrium, ii) no products are initially present.

parts.label: 3.1b
parts.statement:
Choose the appropriate way(s) to increase the cyclohexanol yield. Tick the relevant boxes.

□ Increase the temperature up to 50 °C using a reflux.

□ Increase the temperature up to 60 °C, evaporating (distilling) the acetone.

□ Add some ethanol to the reaction mixture.

□ Add some ethanal to the reaction mixture.

Often the rate-limiting step in the MSPV reaction is the hydride transfer or the alcoholysis of the alkoxide after hydride transfer. For these two cases, using the above mechanism (2), derive an expression for the rate of reaction as a function of current concentrations of a carbonyl compound, isopropanol and a catalyst. In both cases determine the rate orders in the reactants and the catalyst. Assume that all reaction steps before the limiting step are fast and reversible. Use equilibrium approximation, if necessary. For brevity use the following notation: A for carbonyl compound, B for isopropanol, C for catalyst. Denote intermediates as you wish.
parts.statementAfter:
MSPV reaction can be used to obtain chiral alcohols, if the chiral catalyst is employed. For instance, Campbell et al. used the catalyst based on the chiral 2,2′-dihydroxy-1,1′-binaphtyl (BINOL), which is synthesized in situ from binaphtol and trimethylaluminium:

[figure: p3-fig3]

The chirality of BINOL is due to the sterically hindered rotation around the C–C bond. Though perfectly stable at room temperature, BINOL may racemize when heated.

parts.statement:
Which of the phenols below can form stable (at room temperature) enantiomers so that they can be used in the same fashion to produce a chiral catalyst? Tick the relevant boxes.

[figure: p3-fig4]
parts.statementAfter: Enantiomeric excess, ee, is used to characterize the enantiomeric purity of the substance. This quantity equals to the ratio of the difference of concentrations of enantiomers R and S to their sum: ee = ([R] − [S])/([R] + [S]). Enantiomeric excess of the pure R isomer is unity, ee of the racemic mixture is zero.

parts.statement: When using the enantiomerically pure (BINOL)Al(OiPr) as a catalyst for reduction of α-bromoacetophenone, the ee of the product equals 81%. What is the ee of the product if the catalyst ee equals 50%? Provide your calculation with an illustration or derivation of the final formula.

solution.statement:
**3.1a** Reaction enthalpy ΔrH°₂₉₈ = ΔfH°₂₉₈(C₃H₆O) + ΔfH°₂₉₈(C₆H₁₂O) − ΔfH°₂₉₈(C₃H₈O) − ΔfH°₂₉₈(C₆H₁₀O) = (−248.4)+(−348.2)−(−318.1)−(−271.2) = −7.3 kJ mol⁻¹.

Reaction entropy ΔrS°₂₉₈ = S°₂₉₈(C₃H₆O)+S°₂₉₈(C₆H₁₂O)−S°₂₉₈(C₃H₈O)−S°₂₉₈(C₆H₁₀O) = 200.4+203.4−180.6−229.0 = −5.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Reaction Gibbs energy ΔrG°₂₉₈ = ΔrH°₂₉₈ − TΔrS°₂₉₈ = −5.6 kJ mol⁻¹. Equilibrium constant K = exp(−ΔrG°₂₉₈/RT) = 9.6.

K = x(C₃H₆O)x(C₆H₁₂O)/[x(C₃H₈O)x(C₆H₁₀O)] = ν(C₃H₆O)ν(C₆H₁₂O)/[ν(C₃H₈O)ν(C₆H₁₀O)], where x is molar fraction and ν the amount of substance in the equilibrium mixture. Let initial cyclohexanone amount be y. A 99% yield requires 99% to react, so equilibrium amounts of C₆H₁₀O and C₆H₁₂O are 0.01y and 0.99y. Let initial isopropanol amount be z. Reaction stoichiometry gives equilibrium C₃H₆O = 0.99y and C₃H₈O = z−0.99y. Substitution yields K = (0.99y×0.99y)/[0.01y(z−0.99y)] = 98.01/(z/y−0.99) = 9.6; hence z/y = 11.2.

The mole ratio ν(C₃H₈O):ν(C₆H₁₀O) is 11.2. The mass ratio m(C₃H₈O)/m(C₆H₁₀O) = ν(C₃H₈O)M(C₃H₈O)/[ν(C₆H₁₀O)M(C₆H₁₀O)] = 11.2×60/98 = 6.9.

**3.1b** Selected: ☑ increase temperature to 60 °C, evaporating (distilling) acetone; ☑ add ethanol. The 50 °C reflux and ethanal options are not selected.

**3.2 i) Rate-limiting hydride transfer:** A+C ⇌ A·C (fast, K); A·C → A′·C′ (rate-determining, k). K = [A·C]/([A][C]); rate r = k[A·C] = kK[A][C]. Orders: carbonyl compound 1; isopropanol 0; catalyst 1.

**ii) Rate-limiting transalkoxylation of the alcoholate by isopropanol:** A+C ⇌ A·C (fast, K₁); A·C ⇌ A′·C′ (fast, K₂); A′·C′+B → P (rate-determining, k). K₁ = [A·C]/([A][C]); K₂ = [A′·C′]/[A·C]. Rate r = k[A′·C′][B] = kK₁K₂[A][B][C]. Orders: carbonyl compound 1; isopropanol 1; catalyst 1.

**3.3 — Native completed structural table, continuing on the next source page:**

[figure: p3-sol-fig2]

**3.4 — Solution 1**

The total kinetic scheme is:

[figure: p3-sol-fig3]

According to the scheme the R:S ratio is [(R)product]/[(S)product] = (k[(R)catalyst]+k′[(S)catalyst])/(k[(S)catalyst]+k′[(R)catalyst]). Insert into the ee definition:

ee_product = ([(R)product]−[(S)product])/([(R)product]+[(S)product]) = ([(R)product]/[(S)product]−1)/([(R)product]/[(S)product]+1)

= ((k[(R)catalyst]+k′[(S)catalyst])−(k[(S)catalyst]+k′[(R)catalyst]))/((k[(R)catalyst]+k′[(S)catalyst])+(k[(S)catalyst]+k′[(R)catalyst]))

= (([(R)catalyst]−[(S)catalyst])/([(R)catalyst]+[(S)catalyst]))×(k−k′)/(k+k′) = ee_catalyst×(k−k′)/(k+k′).

Thus product ee is proportional to catalyst ee; ee_product = 0.50×0.81 = 0.41.

**Solution 2**

50% ee ≡ 50% racemic + 50% R. R catalyst → 90.5% R + 9.5% S; racemic catalyst → 50% R + 50% S. R product fraction = 0.5×0.905+0.5×0.5 = 0.7025; S fraction = 0.5×0.095+0.5×0.5 = 0.2975; ee_product = 0.7025−0.2975 = 0.405. Answer: 41%.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 4 — A simple inorganic experiment
problems.statement: Compound A which contains metal X is a colourless crystalline solid and highly soluble in water. It is used as a reagent in analysis and gives in alkali media a binary compound B containing 6.9% (mass) of oxygen. Under heating A decomposes with a mass loss of 36.5%.

parts.statement: Determine the metal X and compounds A and B.
parts.statementAfter: Upon adding some amount of sodium thiosulfate to the solution of A the colour immediately becomes red, then changes to reddish-brown, and after some minutes a dark-brown precipitate C forms (reaction 1). The solution over it is colourless. Being heated on air at 600 °C, C gives a grey powder X (reaction 2), so as 0.90 g of residue can be obtained from 1.10 g of C. A gas evolved by heating C in vacuum (reaction 3) can be absorbed by calcium hydroxide suspension (reaction 4). Being stored for a long time under saturated solution of barium perchlorate in HClO₄ (c = 0.1 mol dm⁻³), the colour of the precipitate becomes lighter, while the use of magnesium perchlorate does not give such an effect.

parts.statement: What is C? Write the equations of the reactions 1–4.
parts.statementAfter: The compound C being stored under the mother liquor (containing an excess of A) changes its colour to yellow due to the transformation into D. If barium ions are added to the suspension of C in the mother liquor, a mixture of D and of a white precipitate is formed.

parts.statement: Propose the formula of D, taking into account that it contains 77.5 mass% of X. Give the equation of D formation.

solution.statement:
**4.1** A general binary formula is XO_n. Molar ratios X:O should be (93.1/A_r(X)):(6.9/16) = 1/n, where n = 0.5; 1; 1.5; 2; etc. n = 0.5 gives A_r(X) = 107.9, silver's relative atomic mass. X = Ag, B = Ag₂O. Heating silver salts generally reduces the metal. From the mass loss, A has molar mass 170 g mol⁻¹, corresponding to silver nitrate: A = AgNO₃.

**4.2** The heated residue in air is metallic silver, since silver compounds readily decompose. C contains silver and probably sulfur/oxygen because it evolves sulfur oxide when heated in vacuum. 1.10 g C contains 0.90 g Ag, so 1 mol Ag occurs in 132 g C. Mass of other elements 132−108 = 24 g corresponds to ½S and ½O: empirical formula AgS₁/₂O₁/₂ or Ag₂SO.

The light-brown precipitate after barium addition means barium sulfate forms, insoluble in acids. Surface sulfate groups are replaced by perchlorate ions from solution. Based on Ag₂SO and sulfate presence, formula Ag₈S₃SO₄ can be suggested.

Equation 1: 16AgNO₃ + 6Na₂S₂O₃ + 6H₂O → 2[Ag₈S₃]SO₄↓ + 4Na₂SO₄ + 4NaNO₃ + 12HNO₃.

Equation 2: [Ag₈S₃]SO₄ + 2O₂ → 8Ag + 4SO₂.

Equation 3: [Ag₈S₃]SO₄ → 2Ag₂S + 4Ag + 2SO₂.

Equation 4: SO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ = CaSO₃ + H₂O, or 2SO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ = Ca(HSO₃)₂.

**4.3** Assume nitrate substitutes sulfate ions in C. For a formula unit with n silver atoms, molar mass = 108n/0.775 = 139.35n. n = 3 gives M = 418 g mol⁻¹; 418−108×3 = 94 corresponds to NO₃+S. D = [Ag₃S]NO₃. Equation: [Ag₈S₃]SO₄ + AgNO₃ + 2NaNO₃ → 3[Ag₃S]NO₃ + Na₂SO₄.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 5 — Simple estimates of graphene properties
problems.statement:
Graphene is a two-dimensional, one atom thick carbon material (Fig. 1 a). Many layers of graphene stack together to form graphite (Fig. 1 b).

[figure: p5-fig1]

Fig. 1. (a) The structure of graphene. Spheres are carbon atoms. They are arranged in hexagons. The area of one carbon hexagon is 5.16·10⁻²⁰ m². (b) Crystal lattice of graphite. Three graphene layers are shown.

Such atomic structure was long considered to be unstable. However, in 2004 Andrey Geim and Konstantin Novoselov have reported production of the first samples of this unusual material. This groundbreaking invention was awarded by Nobel prize in 2010.

Experimental studies of graphene are still restricted. Production of massive portions of the new substance still is a challenging synthetic problem. Many properties of graphene were estimated. Usually, there is not enough information for rigorous calculations, so we have to make assumptions and neglect unimportant factors. In this problem, you will estimate the adsorption properties of graphene.

parts.statement: Estimate the specific surface of graphene open for adsorption in units m² g⁻¹. Consider that graphene plane is separated from any other solid or liquid substance.
parts.statementAfter:
The single layer of nitrogen molecules adsorbed on the outer surface of graphite is shown in Fig. 2. Assume that the same arrangement of nitrogen molecules is formed on a graphene surface.

[figure: p5-fig2]

Fig. 2. Nitrogen molecules N₂ (grey circles) on the outer surface of graphite.

parts.statement: How many grams of nitrogen can be adsorbed on 1 gram of graphene assuming that the graphene layer is placed onto the surface of a solid support? Estimate the volume occupied by these nitrogen molecules after the complete desorption from 1 g of graphene (pressure 1 bar, temperature 298 K).
parts.statementAfter:
Let us consider adsorption as a common chemical equilibrium

A_gas ⇌ A_ads, (1)

(A_gas are molecules A in the gaseous state, A_ads are the same molecules on the surface) with the equilibrium constant K:

K = n_A ads (mol m⁻²) / p_A gas (bar).

(Such an assumption holds if a small number of molecules is adsorbed on the surface.)

Adsorption properties of graphene can be estimated from the data for adsorption on a regular three-dimensional graphite. The enthalpy of adsorption (ΔH° of reaction (1)) of any molecule A on graphene is on average by 10% less negative compared to that on graphite. On graphite, the adsorbed molecule is bound more strongly due to the interaction with the lower graphene layers in the lattice (Fig. 1b) and hence the enthalpy of adsorption is more negative. The standard entropies of adsorption on graphene and graphite are assumed to be the same.

parts.statement: How many moles of CCl₄ are adsorbed on 1 g of graphene at p(CCl₄) = 10⁻⁴ bar if 2.0·10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² of CCl₄ are adsorbed on graphite at p(CCl₄) = 6.6·10⁻⁵ bar? Assume that the graphene is placed onto the surface of a solid support and that the interaction of CCl₄ with the solid support does not change the enthalpy of adsorption of CCl₄ on graphene. The temperature in both cases is 293 K. The enthalpy of adsorption of CCl₄ on graphite is −35.1 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.statementAfter: Graphene was proposed as a gas sensor to detect very small amounts of gases. If 10⁹ particles of gas are adsorbed on 1 cm² of graphene surface this is enough to measure the change in electric resistivity of the graphene layer and to detect the presence of gas.

parts.statement:
Determine the minimal content of ethane in air (in mol%) that can be detected with a graphene sensor at 293 K. The known data for the adsorption of alkanes on graphite are shown in Fig. 3. Assume that the air does not affect the adsorption of ethane. Assume atmospheric pressure.

[figure: p5-fig3]

[figure: p5-fig4]

Fig. 3. (a) Equilibrium constants of adsorption of alkanes on graphite surface at 293 K. ln K [mol m⁻² bar⁻¹] is plotted versus ln M (molar mass in g mol⁻¹). (b) Enthalpies of adsorption of alkanes on graphite surface. ΔH° is plotted versus ln M. Both dependencies are linear.

solution.statement:
**5.1** The area of a hexagon is S = 5.16·10⁻²⁰ m². Number of hexagons per gram of carbon: n = N_A×(3/6)×(1/12) = 6.022·10²³×0.5×(1/12) = 2.51·10²². Area per gram: S_total = S×n×2 = 5.16·10⁻²⁰×2.51·10²²×2 = 2590 m² g⁻¹. In a two-dimensional material both sides of the layer are open for adsorption and must be considered; multiply total hexagon area by two!

**5.2** Graphene is on the solid support, so only one side of the plane works. One nitrogen molecule falls on six carbon atoms (three hexagons), as in Fig. 2. m(N₂)/m(C) = (1×28)/(6×12) = 0.39; m(N₂) = 0.39 g. V(N₂) = [(m/M)RT]/p = [(0.39/28)×8.314×298]/100 = 0.34 dm³.

**5.3** K(graphite) = n(CCl₄ on graphite)/p(CCl₄) = (2.0·10⁻⁷)/(6.6·10⁻⁵) = 3.0·10⁻³ mol m⁻² bar⁻¹. Recalculate for graphene: adsorption enthalpies differ by 10%, entropies are the same. K(graphene)/K(graphite) = exp[−(ΔH_graphene−ΔH_graphite)/(RT)] = exp[−3510/(8.314×293)] = 0.24. Thus K(graphene) = 0.24 K(graphite) = 7.2·10⁻⁴ mol m⁻² bar⁻¹.

Adsorption on graphene is calculated from this constant and its area in m² g⁻¹. Only one side works: S_total = 2590/2 = 1295 m² g⁻¹. n [mol g⁻¹] = K(graphene) [mol m⁻² bar⁻¹] × p(CCl₄) [bar] × S(graphene) [m² g⁻¹] = (7.2·10⁻⁴)×10⁻⁴×1295 = 9.3·10⁻⁵ mol g⁻¹. The area determined in question 5.1 is used here.

**5.4** Lower detectable surface concentration: n [mol m⁻²] = [(1·10⁹)/(6.02·10²³)]/(1·10⁻⁴) = 1.7·10⁻¹¹. From Fig. 3: M = 30; ln M = 3.4; ln K = −11.8; ΔH° = −22.5 kJ mol⁻¹. K(C₂H₆) = 7.5·10⁻⁶ mol m⁻² bar⁻¹.

The printed key says to recalculate this constant for graphene “as in question 5.2”. K(C₂H₆, graphene) = K(C₂H₆, graphite)×exp[−2250/(8.314×293)] = 7.5·10⁻⁶×0.4 = 3.0·10⁻⁶ mol m⁻² bar⁻¹. Partial pressure p(C₂H₆) = n(C₂H₆ on graphene)/K(C₂H₆, graphene) = (1.7·10⁻¹¹)/(3.0·10⁻⁶) = 5.7·10⁻⁶ bar. Content of C₂H₆ = [(5.7·10⁻⁶)/1.013]×100% = 5.6·10⁻⁴%.

*Source cross-reference:* the quoted “5.2” is printed on physical page 249; the enthalpy correction is worked in 5.3. The printed reference is retained.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 6 — Cyclopropanes. So simple. So fancy…
problems.statement:
Cyclopropanes bearing donor and acceptor substituents at the neighbouring C-atoms, for example, A, demonstrate high reactivity behaving similar to 1,3-zwitterion B.

[figure: p6-fig1]

Thus, A1 (X = 4-OMe) undergoes the three-membered ring opening in the Lewis acid-catalyzed reaction with 1,3-dimethoxybenzene as a nucleophile giving the product C.

parts.statement: Write down structural formula of C.
parts.statementAfter: A1 participates in cycloadditions, annulations, oligomerizations, and other processes. Thus, [3+2]-cycloaddition between A1 and 4-methoxybenzaldehyde leads to a five-membered ring in D. Complete decarboxylation of D produces E (C₁₈H₂₀O₃), the molecule of the latter having a plane of symmetry.

parts.statement: Write down structural formulae of D and E indicating their stereochemistry.
parts.statementAfter:
Also, A can undergo various transformations in the absence of any reaction partners except catalysts. Some transformations typical of A1 are shown in the Scheme below.

[figure: p6-fig2]

To determine the structures of F–J, a set of physico-chemical data was obtained (see Table for some results). It was found that:

a) F and G are structural isomers of A1;

b) G is formed as the most stable stereoisomer;

c) H and I are structural isomers;

d) H is formed as a single diastereomer with C₂ axis of symmetry (the molecule looks the same after rotation through the angle of 180°);

e) I is formed as a mixture of two diastereomers;

f) J is naphthalene derivative.

In the process leading to I, one molecule of A1 demonstrates the described above common reactivity (analogous to that of B). The other molecule of A1 behaves differently. Also, the latter behaviour is demonstrated by cyclopropane A2 (dimethyl 2-(3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl)cylopropane-1,1-dicarboxylate) when treated with SnCl₄ in CH₃NO₂ affording K as a mixture of two diastereomers. The major isomer has the centre of symmetry. Similar reactivity is shown by A2 in Sn(OTf)₂-catalyzed reaction with G furnishing L.

| Compound | Non-aromatic CH | CH₂ | CH₃ | OH | Aromatic | Composition |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F | 1 | 1 | 1+1+1 | 0 | 4 in total | C 63.62%, H 6.11% |
| G | 1+1+1 | 0 | 2+1 | 0 | 4 in total | C 63.62%, H 6.11% |
| H | 1 | 1 | 1+1+1 | 0 | 4 in total | C 63.62%, H 6.11% |
| I | 1+1+1 | 1+1 | 2+1+1+1+1 | 0 | 7 in total | C 63.62%, H 6.11% |
| J | 0 | 0 | 1+1 | 1 | 5 in total | C 67.22%, H 5.22% |
| K | 1+1 | 1 | 2+1+1+1 | 0 | 1 | C 59.24%, H 6.23% |
| L | 1+1+1+1+1 | 1 | 2+2+1+1+1+1 | 0 | 5 in total | C 61.21%, H 6.18% |

parts.statement: Write down the structural formulae of F–J, and those of L and the major isomer of K.

solution.statement:
**6.1**

[figure: p6-sol-fig1]

Reaction of A1 with 1,3-dimethoxybenzene as a nucleophile proceeds as Friedel-Crafts alkylation. Electrophiles attacks onto ortho-/para-position. Attack onto C4 position of arene proceeds easier than attack onto sterically more hindered C2 atom.

**6.2**

[figure: p6-sol-fig2]

Compound A1 reacts similarly to 1,3-zwitterion B1. It is the 3-atom component. Therefore, 4-methoxybenzaldehyde is a two-atom component. Benzene ring is not prone to react as two-atom component. So, C=O group participates in the reaction. Accounting for its polarization, carbonyl oxygen reacts with a positive end of 1,3-zwitterion B1.

The product has cis-geometry. Therefore, compound D is cis-dimethyl 2,5-diaryltetrahydrofuran-3,3-dicarboxylate. Decarboxylation of compound D produces 2,5-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)tetrahydrofuran E (accounting for its molecular formula). It has cis-arrangement of aryl groups as E has a plane of symmetry.

**6.3** Compounds F and G are isomers of A1. G has three CH groups instead of the cyclopropane fragment, two equivalent ester groups and unchanged aromatic fragment. Thus G is ArCH=CHCH(CO₂Me)₂, formed by cyclopropane-to-alkene isomerization as the (E)-isomer (more stable than Z). F has CH₂ and CH groups, two different ester groups and unchanged aromatic fragment. F is formed from A1 and undergoes secondary isomerization into G. Therefore F is ArCH₂CH=C(CO₂Me)₂.

I has twice as many protons as A1, so isomeric H and I are dimers of A1. The question directly states that two molecules of A1 react to form I. H is highly symmetric and its aromatic fragment is unchanged. It results from symmetric dimerization where the positive end of B1 of one molecule reacts with the negative end of B1 of the other and vice versa, producing cyclohexane. Its cis-isomer has C₂ symmetry; trans has a centre of symmetry. H is cis.

From symmetry and table data, K is a symmetric dimer of A2. The aromatic/non-aromatic proton ratio in K is less than in A2. Accounting for question 1, benzylic carbon of one A2 reacts as an electrophile with the ortho-position of the other's aromatic fragment (nucleophilic centre), and vice versa. A2 behaves as 1,3-zwitterion B2. K is a 9,10-dihydroanthracene derivative. Its major isomer has a centre of symmetry, hence trans alkyl substituents.

I has seven aromatic protons, one fewer than H in which arene fragments remain intact. One A1 acts as B1 and the other as B2. One new C–C bond is formed by Friedel–Crafts alkylation of the first aromatic group by the positive end of the second 1,3-zwitterion; another forms by coupling electrophilic benzylic carbon of the first with nucleophilic malonate carbon of the second. I is a tetraline derivative.

J has 12 protons. Composition gives C₁₃H₁₂O₄, one C, four H and one O fewer than A1. J has no aliphatic CH/CH₂ groups, only methoxy groups and OH. Under thermal conditions A1 isomerizes into Z-G, which undergoes intramolecular acylation furnishing naphthalene derivative J: methyl 1-hydroxy-7-methoxynaphthalene-2-carboxylate.

[figure: p6-sol-fig3]

L has 36 protons and C₃₀H₃₆O₁₂, so forms from A2 and G. The electrophilic centre of B2 attacks the double bond in G according to Markovnikov's rule. The formed cation adds to the ortho-position of the trimethoxyphenyl group, furnishing the substituted indane L.

[figure: p6-sol-fig4]

problems.title: Theoretical problem 7 — Diverse permanganatometry
problems.statement: The amount of many reducing agents can be determined by permanganatometric titration in alkaline medium allowing permanganate ion reduction to manganate.

parts.statement: Write down the ionic reaction equation for titration of formate with permanganate in an aqueous NaOH solution with a concentration of ~0.5 mol dm⁻³.
parts.statementAfter: Titration with permanganate in alkaline medium is often supplemented by addition of a barium salt, which leads to precipitation of manganate as BaMnO₄.

parts.statement: Which side redox processes involving manganate is suppressed by the barium salt? Write down an example of equation of the corresponding reaction.
parts.statementAfter:
A volume of 10.00 cm³ (V_Mn) of KMnO₄ solution with a concentration of 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ (c_Mn) was placed in each of flasks A, B, and C and different reactions were conducted in each flask.

A sample solution containing crotonic acid (CA) CH₃–CH=CH–COOH, an alkali and barium nitrate (both in an excess) were added to flask A, and the reaction mixture was incubated for 45 min. It is known that crotonic acid loses 10 electrons under the experiment conditions.

parts.label: 7.3a
parts.statement: Write down the total ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.statementAfter:
A volume of 8.00 cm³ (V_CN) of potassium cyanide solution (c_CN = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³) was then added to the incubated mixture. This resulted in completion of the following reaction:

2Ba²⁺ + 2MnO₄⁻ + CN⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2BaMnO₄ + CNO⁻ + H₂O.

BaMnO₄ precipitate was then filtered off, and the excess of cyanide in the filtrate was titrated with AgNO₃ solution (c_Ag = 0.0050 mol dm⁻³) till detectable precipitation was observed. Note that both CN⁻ and CNO⁻ are analogs of halide ions, but CNO⁻ affords soluble silver salt.

parts.label: 7.3b
parts.statement: Give the formula for the complex formed when Ag⁺ ions were initially added to the cyanide solution (until the precipitate was formed).

parts.label: 7.3c
parts.statement: Give the formula of the precipitate formed.

parts.label: 7.3d
parts.statement: Derive the formula for calculating the amount of substance of crotonic acid in the sample solution. Calculate the mass of crotonic acid (in mg) if 5.40 cm³ (V_Ag) of the silver salt solution was consumed for the titration to the endpoint.
parts.statementAfter: Another sample of crotonic acid and alkali (in an excess) were added to flask B, this mixture lacking barium salt. An excess of KI (instead of cyanide) was added as a reducing agent. The mixture was then acidified and the iodine evolved was titrated with a thiosulfate solution (c_S = 0.1000 mol dm⁻³). 4.90 cm³ (V_S1) of the titrant was used to reach the endpoint.

parts.statement: Derive the formula for calculating the amount of substance of crotonic acid in this experiment. Calculate the mass of crotonic acid (in mg).
parts.statementAfter: A sample containing tin(II) was added to flask C, and the medium was adjusted to weak alkaline. Tin(II) was quantitatively oxidized to Sn(OH)₆²⁻, whereas a precipitate formed as a result of permanganate reduction. The precipitate was isolated, washed off, dried at 250 °C, weighed (the mass of the water-free precipitate (m_prec), representing a binary compound, was of 28.6 mg), and dissolved in H₂SO₄ in the presence of an excess of potassium iodide. The evolved iodine was titrated with 0.1000 M thiosulfate solution. 2.5 cm³ (V_S2) of the latter was consumed to attain the endpoint.

parts.label: 7.5a
parts.statement: Write down the reaction of precipitation. Confirm it with calculations.

parts.label: 7.5b
parts.statement: Calculate the mass of tin in the sample (in mg) referred to the metal.

solution.statement:
**7.1** 2MnO₄⁻ + HCOO⁻ + 3OH⁻ → 2MnO₄²⁻ + CO₃²⁻ + 2H₂O.

**7.2** MnO₄²⁻ + 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻; or 3MnO₄²⁻ + 2H₂O → MnO₂ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 4OH⁻.

**7.3a** C₄H₅O₂⁻ + 10MnO₄⁻ + 14OH⁻ + 12Ba²⁺ → 10BaMnO₄ + CH₃COO⁻ + 2BaCO₃ + 8H₂O.

**7.3b** Before the endpoint: [Ag(CN)₂]⁻.

**7.3c** After the endpoint: Ag⁺ + [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ = Ag[Ag(CN)₂]↓, or Ag⁺ + CN⁻ = AgCN↓. Thus Ag[Ag(CN)₂] or AgCN is the correct answer.

**7.3d** Permanganate left after crotonic acid reaction: c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA (mmol). Cyanide consumed for residual permanganate: ½(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA). Cyanide excess: c_CN V_CN − ½(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA).

For the **correct** silver–cyanide stoichiometry (1:2): 2c_Ag V_Ag = c_CN V_CN − ½(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA). Therefore n_CA = [2c_Ag V_Ag − c_CN V_CN + ½c_Mn V_Mn]/5 = [2×0.005×5.40 − 0.0100×8.00 + 0.5×0.0400×10.00]/5 = 0.0348 mmol. m_CA = 0.0348×86.09 = 3.00 mg (M_CA = 86.09 g mol⁻¹).

The native key also explicitly prints an alternative for the **wrong** silver–cyanide stoichiometry (1:1): c_Ag V_Ag = c_CN V_CN − ½(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA); n_CA = [c_Ag V_Ag − c_CN V_CN + ½c_Mn V_Mn]/5 = [0.005×5.40 − 0.0100×8.00 + 0.5×0.0400×10.00]/5 = 0.0290 mmol; m_CA = 0.0290×86.09 = 2.49 mg. This is retained as the source's labelled wrong-stoichiometry alternative.

**7.4** Schematically: 10MnO₄⁻ + 1 crotonate → 10MnO₄²⁻ + products. Remaining permanganate: c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA (mmol). Formed manganate: 10n_CA (mmol). After iodide addition:

2MnO₄⁻ + 10I⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5I₂ + 8H₂O;

MnO₄²⁻ + 4I⁻ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 2I₂ + 4H₂O.

Iodine evolved (mmol I₂): 2.5n_KMnO4 left + 2n_K2MnO4 = 2.5(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA) + 2×10n_CA. 2Na₂S₂O₃ + I₂ = Na₂S₄O₆ + 2NaI. n_Na2S2O3 = 2n_I2 = 5(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA) + 40n_CA. Thus 5(c_Mn V_Mn − 10n_CA) + 40n_CA = c_S V_S1; n_CA = ½c_Mn V_Mn − 0.1c_S V_S1 = (0.5×0.0400×10.00) − (0.1×0.1000×4.90) = 0.151 mmol; m_CA = n_CA M_CA = 13.00 mg.

**7.5a** Oxidation in weak alkaline medium gives an insoluble binary manganese compound. Drying conditions suggest a manganese oxide or mixture. Thiosulfate, iodine and precipitate have the same amount of equivalent: n_eq = V_S2 c_S = 0.1000×2.5 = 0.25 mmol; M_eq = 28.6 mg/0.25 mmol = 114.4 g mol⁻¹, the precipitate's molar mass of equivalent.

Possible cases:

• MnO₂: scheme MnO₄⁻ + Sn²⁺ → MnO₂↓ + Sn⁴⁺. MnO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O; I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. Equivalent molar mass 86.94/2 = 43.47 g mol⁻¹.

• Mn₂O₃: Mn₂O₃ + 2I⁻ + 6H⁺ → I₂ + 2Mn²⁺ + 3H₂O. The native key prints its equivalent molar mass as **157.88/4 = 78.9 g mol⁻¹**. The printed divisor/result disagreement is retained here rather than silently corrected.

• The experimental equivalent molar mass is even higher, so manganese compounds not oxidizing iodide, i.e. manganese(II), may be present. Only manganese(II,III) oxide fits: Mn₃O₄ + 2I⁻ + 8H⁺ → I₂ + 3Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O; equivalent molar mass 228.9/2 = 114.4 g mol⁻¹.

Precipitation: 6MnO₄⁻ + 13[Sn(OH)₄]²⁻ + 16H₂O → 2Mn₃O₄↓ + 13[Sn(OH)₆]²⁻ + 6OH⁻.

**7.5b** Tin amount is 13/2 of that of Mn₃O₄: n_Sn = (28.6/228.9)×(13/2) = 0.812 mmol; m_Sn = 96.4 mg.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 8 — Unique life of archaea
problems.statement:
Archaea (or archaebacteria) are single-celled microorganisms. They significantly differ from bacteria and eukaryotes at the molecular level.

Enzymatic reaction of methylamine with water is the major energy source for some archaea. In a particular experiment, an archaea strain was cultivated at pH 7 under anaerobic (oxygen free) conditions with the nutrient medium containing ¹³CH₃NH₂ as the only energy source. After a certain incubation period, the gas over the archaea culture was sampled and analyzed. It was found that the gas contains two substances, A and B, in a molar ratio of 1:3 correspondingly (the sample density relative to H₂ is 12.0).

parts.statement: Calculate the volume fractions (in %) of A and B in the mixture.
Determine A and B if there are no nitrogen atoms in the gas collected.
Write down the equation of enzymatic reaction of methylamine with water described in the above experiment using predominant form of each species.
parts.statementAfter:
Enzymes containing the residue of α-amino acid X are found in many archaea capable of methylamine utilization. It is known that X:

• is composed of atoms of 4 elements;

• contains 18.8 mass% of oxygen;

• possesses the single individual tRNA and is incorporated into proteins of archaea during translation.

Amino acid L-lysine (see the structure in scheme below) was identified as the X precursor in archaea. All carbon and nitrogen atoms found in X originate from two starting lysine molecules. Different isotope-labelled L-lysines were introduced into a model system to clarify the biosynthetic pathways of X. Results:

| Isotope composition of L-lysine | Molar mass (rounded to integer) of the X residue [RCH(NH₂)CO], bound to tRNA / g mol⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| Normal | 238 |
| All carbons ¹³C, all nitrogens ¹⁵N | 253 |
| ε-amino group with ¹⁵N | 239 |

solution.statement:
**8.1** Volume ratio equals mole ratio (1:3). Volume fractions A = 25%, B = 75%.

**8.2** Mixture molar mass = 12.0×2.0 = 24.0 g mol⁻¹. Both gases having that mass is impossible; one is lighter and the other heavier. Under anaerobic conditions ¹³C-methylamine and water can theoretically yield two nitrogen-free gases lighter than 24.0: H₂ or ¹³CH₄. Possibilities:

| Light gas | Light-gas volume fraction / % | Heavy-gas molar mass / g mol⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|
| H₂ | 25 | 31.3 |
| H₂ | 75 | 90.0 |
| ¹³CH₄ | 25 | 26.3 |
| ¹³CH₄ | 75 | 45.0 |

At neutral cellular pH ammonia is ammonium ion, not gaseous. Only possible variant: A = ¹³C¹⁶O₂ and B = ¹³C¹H₄.

**8.3** 4¹³CH₃NH₃⁺ + 2H₂O → 3¹³CH₄ + ¹³CO₂ + 4NH₄⁺.

**8.4** M(X) = 238+17 (OH group) = 255 g mol⁻¹. Number of oxygen atoms = (255×0.188)/16.00 = 3. Two lysines contain 12 carbon and 4 nitrogen atoms, 16 total. Comparison of isotope table lines 1/2 shows 15 of these 16 atoms occur in X; lines 1/3 show one of the two ε-amino nitrogens is lost. X has 12 C and 3 N. Remaining molar mass 255−12×12−3×14−3×16 = 21 g mol⁻¹ is hydrogen (21 atoms). X = C₁₂H₂₁N₃O₃.

**8.5i** C = C₆H₁₄N₂O₂; D = C₁₂H₂₆N₄O₃; E = C₁₂H₂₃N₃O₄. C is a lysine isomer; 2×C₆H₁₄N₂O₂ = C₁₂H₂₈N₄O₄ enters D synthesis. One water molecule forms in each step: C+lysine → D (C₁₂H₂₈N₄O₄−H₂O = C₁₂H₂₆N₄O₃), and E → X (C₁₂H₂₁N₃O₃+H₂O = C₁₂H₂₃N₃O₄).

**8.5ii** ☑ Oxidative deamination. The native key's loss/gain line at D → E prints **C₁₂H₂₄N₄O₃ − C₁₂H₂₁N₃O₄**, minus NH₃, plus O. Thus oxidative deamination: R–CH₂–NH₂ + [O] → R–CH=O + NH₃ (schematically). *Source discrepancy:* these hydrogen counts differ from D/E in the immediately preceding native table and water-loss calculation; both printed versions are preserved.

**8.6** H bound to carbon 4 or 5 would remove chirality, so H is unambiguously at carbon 3. The amino group preceding heterocyclic nitrogen determines the other substituents. Nitrogen enters the cycle by amino/formyl reaction; the formyl group arises by oxidative deamination. Cycle size indicates the α-amino group. Thus position 3: H; 4: Me; 5: R.

[figure: p8-sol-fig1]

**8.7** Working backwards X → D gives C = (3R)-3-methyl-D-ornithine:

[figure: p8-sol-fig2]

C stereochemistry follows that of the cyclic fragment, with no isomerization from C to X. Either lysine amino group can form a peptide bond with C's carboxyl group, but only ε-amino involvement supplies X as an α-amino acid. X is pyrrolysine, the 22nd amino acid of the genetic code:

[figure: p8-sol-fig3]

**8.8** Completed native form:

[figure: p8-sol-fig4]

A has 1 amino group and 0 oxygen; C has 1 amino and 1 oxygen; G has 1 amino and 1 oxygen; U has 0 amino and 2 oxygen. Two amino groups per three bases suggest one U. The remaining two bases have two amino groups and one oxygen. A is one; either G or C is the last. Selected: A = 1; C = 0 or 1; G = 0 or 1; U = 1.

**8.9a** The fragment has four U, usable to determine the reading frame. The triplet has only one A. UGA/UAG are options; UAG occurs twice. Both are STOP codons in the table, but this is a coding sequence. In definite nucleotide motives STOP codons may incorporate amino acids. Therefore 8 amino acids are encoded (if UGA is STOP, then 7 amino-acid residues):

…AA|UAG|AAU|UAG|CGG|AAC|AGA|GGG|UGA|C…

Number of amino acids = 8.

**8.9b** Only one codon incorporates X; UGA or UAG. More than one X occurs, so it is UAG (twice), while UGA encodes Sec. Sequence: X–Asn–X–Arg–Asn–Arg–Gly–Sec. The native ten-box form retains two empty terminal boxes:

[figure: p8-sol-fig5]
